framing: The exact text a chat model actually receives
paragraphs: An application stores a conversation as a list of messages. A model reads one long line of token IDs. The code between them decides where a request ends, which role speaks next, and whether an answer is finished or still open.

You usually notice this code only when it breaks. A refactor adds a second beginning token or moves a newline, the screen still shows the same question, and the model starts behaving differently for no visible reason. Staring at the weights will not help.

We will render one small forecast conversation three ways: as a finished training row, as a fresh request, and as a partial answer to continue. Then we will look at real token IDs from a real tokenizer, test whether a user can forge a marker, and see how the same format decides which tokens a training run actually scores.

By the end, you will know what to compare first when a chat model regresses, how to keep your training and serving paths in step, and what you can still check when a hosted API applies the template for you.
outcomes: Render finished conversations, fresh requests, and assistant prefills, and explain the difference.
Check whether a user can forge a marker, and spot whitespace and doubled-token bugs.
Check training and serving parity, target masks, stopping, and context budgets.
question: After a serving refactor, how could you tell a changed model from a changed prompt?
